questions.stem: Every morning, my grandfather \_\_\_\_ a long walk in the park.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Every morning' marks a repeated habit, and habits use the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'is taking' is present continuous, which means right now, not every day. Misconception: treating the continuous as an all-purpose present.
- **(C)** 'took' is simple past, a single finished event, not a repeated routine. Misconception: ignoring the habitual marker.
- **(D)** 'has taken' is present perfect and needs present relevance, not a daily habit. Misconception: reaching for the perfect without a reason.

**Principle:** Repeated or habitual actions take the simple present, often with adverbs like every day, usually, always.

**Intuition hook:** If it happens like clockwork, keep the verb plain and simple.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: Fill the blank with the correct form of the verb in brackets. — Water \_\_\_\_ (boil) at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A scientific fact that is always true takes the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'is boiling' (continuous) wrongly suggests it is happening at this moment rather than always. Misconception: using the continuous for a permanent truth.
- 'boiled' (past) wrongly places a timeless fact in finished time. Misconception: attaching tense to a fact that has no time limit.

**Principle:** General truths and scientific facts use the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** Facts that are always true live in the plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: Look! The baby \_\_\_\_ at you.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Look!' points to an action happening at this very moment, so the present continuous is required.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'smiles' is a habit, not something happening now. Misconception: using simple present for an action in progress.
- **(C)** 'smiled' is finished past, but the baby is smiling right now. Misconception: mismatching the moment of speaking.
- **(D)** 'smile' does not agree with the singular subject and is not a finite present form here. Misconception: dropping the -s and the auxiliary.

**Principle:** Actions in progress at the moment of speaking use am/is/are + -ing.

**Intuition hook:** 'Look!' or 'Listen!' almost always means an -ing action is happening now.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: Yesterday, our class \_\_\_\_ (visit) the science museum.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Yesterday' names a finished time, so the completed action takes the simple past.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'have visited' (present perfect) clashes with a stated finished time; you cannot say 'have visited yesterday'. Misconception: using present perfect with a definite past time.
- 'was visiting' (past continuous) would need an interruption or background frame that is not here. Misconception: adding an -ing without a reason.

**Principle:** A completed action at a definite past time uses the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** A finished time word like 'yesterday' locks the verb into the simple past.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

fields.Cognitive skill: Matching finished time to simple past

questions.stem: By the time we reached the hall, the concert \_\_\_\_.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Two past events are compared. The concert starting happened before we reached, so it takes the past perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'already started' drops the auxiliary 'had' that marks the earlier event. Misconception: forgetting the 'had' that signals 'first past'.
- **(C)** 'has already started' is present perfect and cannot sit before another past point. Misconception: mixing present perfect into a past timeline.
- **(D)** 'starts' is present and ignores that everything here is in the past. Misconception: losing track of the timeline entirely.

**Principle:** When two past events are compared, the earlier one takes the past perfect (had + past participle).

**Intuition hook:** The 'first past' event wears the 'had' badge.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: She \_\_\_\_ (live) in this city since 2019.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Since 2019' marks a state that began in the past and still continues, so the present perfect is used.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'lived' (simple past) would wrongly suggest she no longer lives there. Misconception: treating an ongoing state as finished.
- 'is living' alone cannot take 'since 2019' to mean the whole stretch up to now. Misconception: using a plain continuous where duration-to-now is meant.

**Principle:** A state or action beginning in the past and continuing to now uses the present perfect, especially with 'since'.

**Intuition hook:** 'Since' plus 'still true today' equals has/have + past participle.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: 'You look worried. Don't panic — I \_\_\_\_ help you with your project.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The speaker decides to help at the moment of speaking, and a spontaneous offer or promise uses 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'am helping' suggests a fixed prior arrangement, but this is a decision made on the spot. Misconception: confusing a plan with an offer.
- **(B)** 'help' is simple present and cannot express this future promise. Misconception: using present for a future decision.
- **(D)** 'helped' is past, but the help has not happened yet. Misconception: wrong direction in time.

**Principle:** Offers, promises, and decisions made at the moment of speaking use 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** A promise made on the spot rides on 'will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: Quiet, please! The students \_\_\_\_ (write) a test right now.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Right now' marks an action in progress, so the present continuous is used.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'write' (simple present) would mean a habit, not this moment. Misconception: using simple present for an ongoing action.
- 'wrote' (simple past) contradicts 'right now'. Misconception: mismatching the present moment.

**Principle:** Use the present continuous for an action happening at the moment of speaking.

**Intuition hook:** 'Right now' is a green light for -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: My mother \_\_\_\_ to work by metro every single day.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Every single day' marks a habit, and habits use the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'is going' means now or a temporary phase, not a daily routine. Misconception: continuous used for a permanent habit.
- **(C)** 'has gone' suggests she has left and is away now, not a routine. Misconception: reading a habit as a present result.
- **(D)** 'went' is a single finished trip, not a repeated pattern. Misconception: past used for a habit.

**Principle:** Daily routines use the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** 'Every day' is the plain present's home turf.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: The sun \_\_\_\_ (rise) in the east and \_\_\_\_ (set) in the west.
questions.solution:
**Why:** These are permanent natural truths, so both verbs take the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'is rising / is setting' would wrongly limit a permanent truth to this moment. Misconception: using continuous for a general truth.
- 'rose / set' would wrongly place a timeless fact in the past. Misconception: adding past time to an always-true statement.

**Principle:** Permanent, always-true statements use the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** If it was true yesterday and will be true tomorrow, use the plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Warm-Up: Core Tense Recognition

questions.stem: I \_\_\_\_ the answer to this difficult question.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Know' is a stative verb (a state of mind), so it uses the simple present and normally rejects the -ing form.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'am knowing' forces a state into the continuous. Misconception: treating every present idea as an -ing action.
- **(C)** 'have been knowing' piles the continuous onto a stative verb. Misconception: over-applying the perfect continuous.
- **(D)** 'knows' does not agree with 'I'. Misconception: subject–verb mismatch.

**Principle:** Stative verbs (know, believe, own, understand) describe states, not actions, and normally avoid the continuous.

**Intuition hook:** You cannot be 'in the middle of knowing'. You simply know.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Read the two sentences. (1) 'My cousin is staying with us this week.' (2) 'My cousin stays with us.' Which sentence shows a temporary, short-term visit?
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present continuous ('is staying') with 'this week' marks a temporary situation; the simple present ('stays') states a general or repeated fact.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'stays' describes a habit or permanent arrangement, not a one-week visit. Misconception: reading the simple present as temporary.
- **(C)** The two forms carry different meanings, so they are not equal. Misconception: assuming the tenses are interchangeable.
- **(D)** Sentence 1 clearly signals temporariness. Misconception: missing the temporary marker.

**Principle:** Present continuous = temporary; simple present = permanent or habitual.

**Intuition hook:** '-ing' for the short term; plain present for the long term.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: We \_\_\_\_ (be) close friends since primary school.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Since primary school' marks a state that began in the past and continues to now, so use the present perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'are friends since' is a very common error; the simple present cannot express a stretch of time up to now. Misconception: using the present simple with 'since'.
- 'were friends' would suggest the friendship has ended. Misconception: treating an ongoing state as finished.

**Principle:** A state continuing from the past up to now uses the present perfect, especially with 'since' or 'for'.

**Intuition hook:** 'Since' + still true today = have/has been.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence correctly: 'I am not understanding this chapter at all.'
questions.answer: I do not understand this chapter at all.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Understand' is a stative verb of mental state, so it takes the simple present, not the continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'am not understanding' forces a state into the -ing form. Misconception: applying the continuous to a verb of mental state.

**Principle:** Verbs of thinking and perceiving (understand, know, realise) are usually stative and avoid the continuous.

**Intuition hook:** Understanding is a state you are in, not an action you perform.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: 'Where is Meera?' 'She \_\_\_\_ to the dentist — she will be back by five.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Has gone to' means she went and is still there (not back yet), which fits 'she will be back by five'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'has been to' means she went and has already returned, which contradicts 'will be back by five'. Misconception: confusing 'have gone' (still away) with 'have been' (already returned).
- **(C)** 'is going' describes an action in progress or an arrangement, not where she is now. Misconception: mismatching the question 'where is she?'
- **(D)** 'goes' is a habit, not this single situation. Misconception: using the simple present for a one-time result.

**Principle:** 'Have gone (to)' = went and still there; 'have been (to)' = went and came back.

**Intuition hook:** Gone means still gone; been means back again.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Which of these sentences are correct as written? Choose ALL that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: 'I am living in a hotel until my new flat is ready.'

options.label: C
options.text: 'The Earth is going around the Sun.'

options.label: D
options.text: 'These days, I am walking to school because my bus route changed.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** Sentence A uses the present continuous for a genuinely temporary situation; sentence D uses it for a temporary change of routine. Both are correct.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'own' is stative, so 'am owning' is wrong; it should be 'I own three bicycles'. Misconception: continuous with a possession verb.
- **(C)** The Earth orbiting the Sun is a permanent fact and needs the simple present ('goes'); 'is going' wrongly makes an eternal truth temporary. Misconception: continuous for a permanent scientific truth.

**Principle:** Use the present continuous only for temporary or in-progress situations, never for stative verbs or permanent facts.

**Intuition hook:** If it is always true or is a state, drop the -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Filtering multiple present-tense uses at once

questions.stem: Explain why this sounds wrong in careful English, and give the corrected sentence: 'I am really liking this new song.'
questions.answer: 'Like' is a stative verb (a feeling), so standard English uses the simple present: 'I really like this new song.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** Verbs of liking and feeling (like, love, hate, prefer) describe states and normally avoid the continuous. (Note: casual slogans such as 'I'm loving it' bend this rule for effect, but careful/standard English keeps the simple present.)

**Distractor analysis:**

- Accepting the -ing form treats a feeling as an ongoing action. Misconception: applying the continuous to a stative feeling verb.

**Principle:** Stative verbs of emotion take the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** Feelings are states you are in, so keep them plain and simple.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: My eyes really hurt. I \_\_\_\_ at this screen for three hours without a break.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present perfect continuous stresses an activity that has continued up to now and explains a present result (sore eyes).

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'have stared' stresses completion or a count, not the ongoing three-hour activity that caused the pain. Misconception: using the plain present perfect where duration up to now is meant.
- **(C)** 'am staring' ignores the three-hour stretch leading up to now. Misconception: present continuous with no sense of duration.
- **(D)** 'stared' cuts the action off from the present, but the eyes hurt right now. Misconception: detaching a past-to-now action from the present.

**Principle:** Present perfect continuous = an action in progress from the past up to now, often explaining a present state.

**Intuition hook:** 'I have been -ing for \[time\]' explains why things are the way they are right now.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Normally I sleep very well, but these days I \_\_\_\_ (not / sleep) properly because of the exams.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The contrast with 'normally' plus 'these days ... because of the exams' marks a temporary situation, so use the present continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'do not sleep' (simple present) would wrongly claim this is a permanent habit, contradicting 'normally I sleep well'. Misconception: using the simple present for a temporary change.

**Principle:** A temporary change from one's usual habit uses the present continuous.

**Intuition hook:** 'These days' signals a passing phase, so reach for -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct for a bicycle you got as a child and still own today?

options.label: A
options.text: 'I have had this bicycle since I was eight.'

options.label: B
options.text: 'I have this bicycle since I was eight.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** A period of possession running from the past up to now uses the present perfect ('have had'), even though 'have' is a stative verb.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'have ... since' with the simple present cannot express a span up to now; it should be 'have had'. Misconception: using the present simple of 'have' with 'since'.

**Principle:** Duration up to now uses the present perfect, even with stative verbs like 'have' (possess).

**Intuition hook:** For 'since / for + now', upgrade 'have' to 'have had'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect with a stative verb

questions.stem: 'You keep changing your answer! What \_\_\_\_ you actually \_\_\_\_?'
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Believe' is stative, so the present-tense question uses 'do you believe', not the continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'are you believing' forces a stative verb into the continuous. Misconception: -ing with a mental-state verb.
- **(C)** 'have you believed' shifts the meaning to a completed idea. Misconception: swapping in the present perfect.
- **(D)** 'did you believe' points to the past, but the situation is happening now. Misconception: wrong time reference.

**Principle:** Stative verbs form present questions with do/does + base verb, not with the continuous.

**Intuition hook:** 'What do you believe?' – never 'What are you believing?'
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Rewrite as ONE sentence using the present perfect continuous, keeping the meaning: 'Mr. Rao started coaching our team in January. He is still coaching us now.'
questions.answer: Mr. Rao has been coaching our team since January.
questions.solution:
**Why:** An action that began in the past and continues now, with focus on the ongoing activity, uses the present perfect continuous with 'since'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'Mr. Rao is coaching since January' wrongly uses a plain continuous for a stretch up to now. Misconception: dropping the perfect from a since-phrase.
- 'Mr. Rao coaches since January' uses the simple present with 'since', which is incorrect. Misconception: present simple + since.

**Principle:** Present perfect continuous joins a past start to an ongoing present activity.

**Intuition hook:** Started then + still going now = has/have been -ing since.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: For which situation is 'I have lived in Pune since 2020' the correct sentence (rather than 'I lived in Pune in 2020')?

options.label: A
options.text: You moved to Pune in 2020 and you still live there today.

options.label: B
options.text: You lived in Pune during 2020 only and later moved away.

options.label: C
options.text: You are planning to move to Pune next year.

options.label: D
options.text: You visited Pune once for a week in 2020.

questions.solution:
**Why:** The present perfect with 'since' means the state started in the past and continues to the present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** A finished stay needs the simple past, 'I lived in Pune in 2020'. Misconception: using the present perfect for a closed past period.
- **(C)** A future plan needs a future form, not the present perfect. Misconception: mapping the perfect onto the future.
- **(D)** A single finished visit uses the simple past. Misconception: perfect for a one-off past event.

**Principle:** Present perfect = past action or state with a continuing link to now.

**Intuition hook:** If it is still true today, choose 'have lived', not 'lived'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Mapping tense to a real situation

questions.stem: The speaker is complaining about an irritating, repeated habit: 'He \_\_\_\_ his phone somewhere; it drives me crazy!'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present continuous with 'always' expresses a repeated action that annoys the speaker, adding an emotional colour that the neutral simple present does not.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'always loses' is a neutral statement of fact; it is grammatical, but it does not carry the complaining tone the context calls for. Misconception: missing that 'is always -ing' signals irritation.
- **(C)** 'has always lost' points to a completed record, not an ongoing irritation. Misconception: perfect for a live complaint.
- **(D)** 'lost' is a single past event. Misconception: past for a repeated habit.

**Principle:** Present continuous + always/constantly/forever expresses a repeated, often annoying, habit.

**Intuition hook:** 'He is always losing it' = the complaint version; 'he always loses it' = the neutral fact.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: No tea for me, thanks. I \_\_\_\_ (prefer) coffee in the mornings.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Prefer' is a stative verb of choice and feeling, so it uses the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'am preferring' forces a stative verb into the continuous. Misconception: -ing with a preference verb.

**Principle:** Verbs of preference (prefer, want, need) are stative and take the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** Preferring is a settled state, so keep it plain.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Are both acceptable in standard English? (1) 'I have known Aisha for five years.' (2) 'I know Aisha for five years.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** Duration up to now with the stative verb 'know' requires the present perfect: 'have known ... for five years'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'I know Aisha for five years' is a classic error; the simple present cannot carry 'for five years' up to now. Misconception: present simple + for-duration.
- **(C)** The two are not equal, since (2) is ungrammatical. Misconception: assuming both are fine.
- **(D)** Sentence (1) is correct, so 'neither' is wrong. Misconception: rejecting a correct present perfect.

**Principle:** 'For / since + up to now' with a stative verb still requires the present perfect.

**Intuition hook:** 'I have known her for years' – never 'I know her for years'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect vs. present simple with duration

questions.stem: Correct this sentence: 'She has never wrote a poem before.'
questions.answer: She has never written a poem before.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present perfect needs the past participle 'written', not the simple past 'wrote'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'wrote' mixes the simple past into a present perfect frame. Misconception: using the past-tense form (wrote) where the participle (written) is required.

**Principle:** Present perfect = has/have + past participle. For irregular verbs, the participle differs from the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** After 'has/have', use the third column: write → wrote → written.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Participle form inside the present perfect

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: 'I have visited the Taj Mahal last year.'

options.label: B
options.text: 'I visited the Taj Mahal last year.'

options.label: C
options.text: 'I am visiting the Taj Mahal last year.'

options.label: D
options.text: 'I visit the Taj Mahal last year.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Last year' is a definite finished time, which requires the simple past.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** The present perfect cannot combine with a specific finished time like 'last year'. Misconception: 'have visited' + a dated past time.
- **(C)** The present continuous cannot take 'last year'. Misconception: -ing form with finished past time.
- **(D)** The simple present cannot describe a finished past event. Misconception: present for a past action.

**Principle:** A finished, dated past time requires the simple past, not the present perfect.

**Intuition hook:** If you can point to when (last year, in 2019), use the simple past.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect vs. simple past with a time marker

questions.stem: A tourist asks a shopkeeper, 'How long are you living in this town?' The shopkeeper looks confused. Explain the problem and give the correct question.
questions.answer: To ask about time up to now, use the present perfect: 'How long have you lived (or have you been living) in this town?'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present continuous 'are you living' suggests a temporary phase or the near future, not the whole span of time up to the present. Duration questions about now use the present perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping the present continuous asks about a temporary or future situation, not lifelong residence. Misconception: using the present continuous for duration up to now.

**Principle:** 'How long' questions about the present use have/has + past participle.

**Intuition hook:** For 'how long up to now', reach for 'have you ...ed', not 'are you ...ing'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Duration questions with the present perfect

questions.stem: A live cricket commentator describes fast action: 'Sharma \_\_\_\_ the ball... and he \_\_\_\_ it straight to the boundary!' Which forms are typical of quick live commentary?
questions.solution:
**Why:** Live commentary conventionally uses the simple present for rapid, complete-in-the-moment actions, as in 'he passes, he shoots, he scores'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** The present continuous suits longer background action ('Sharma is running in to bowl'), not the sharp, finished strike. Misconception: -ing for every live action.
- **(C)** The simple past would narrate the game after the fact, not as it happens. Misconception: past tense for live action.
- **(D)** The present perfect stresses result and relevance, not the quick sequence of live play. Misconception: perfect for live commentary.

**Principle:** Sports and event commentary uses the simple present for quick, sequential, completed actions.

**Intuition hook:** 'He shoots, he scores' – commentary lives in the plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Please do not disturb her. She \_\_\_\_ (talk) to the principal at the moment.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'At the moment' marks an action in progress, so use the present continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'talks' (simple present) would mean a habit, not this moment. Misconception: simple present for an action happening now.

**Principle:** Present continuous for an action in progress at the moment of speaking.

**Intuition hook:** 'At the moment' points straight at -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: In which sentence is the -ing form correct?

options.label: B
options.text: 'I am thinking about the problem right now.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Think about (= consider)' is a dynamic mental process and takes the continuous; understand, know, and want are stative and reject the -ing form.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'understand' is stative; use 'I understand the lesson now'. Misconception: continuous with a state of understanding.
- **(C)** 'know' is stative; use 'I know the answer'. Misconception: continuous with a knowledge verb.
- **(D)** 'want' is stative; use 'I want a short break'. Misconception: continuous with a desire verb.

**Principle:** A verb can be dynamic (an action, e.g. thinking = considering) or stative (a state); only dynamic uses take the continuous.

**Intuition hook:** 'Thinking about' is doing something in your head; 'knowing / wanting / understanding' are just states.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Dynamic vs. stative senses of verbs

questions.stem: In which situation is 'Ravi is working at a bank' the better choice (rather than 'Ravi works at a bank')?

options.label: A
options.text: It is Ravi's permanent, long-term profession.

options.label: B
options.text: Ravi is a student, but he has a temporary summer job at a bank.

options.label: C
options.text: You are naming the career Ravi has chosen for life.

options.label: D
options.text: Ravi retired years ago and no longer works.

questions.solution:
**Why:** The present continuous marks a temporary job; the simple present marks a permanent one.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** A permanent profession uses the simple present, 'Ravi works at a bank'. Misconception: continuous for a permanent job.
- **(C)** A settled career choice is a general fact, so use the simple present. Misconception: continuous for a stable fact.
- **(D)** If he no longer works, the present continuous is simply false. Misconception: present continuous for something not happening.

**Principle:** Present continuous = temporary situation; simple present = permanent situation.

**Intuition hook:** Summer job now = 'is working'; life-long career = 'works'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

questions.stem: 'Do not offer him lunch — he \_\_\_\_ eaten.' (He ate a few minutes ago and is still full.)
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Has just eaten' is the present perfect with 'just', used for a very recent action that has a present result (he is full now). The order is has + just + past participle.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'just has eaten' puts the adverb in the wrong place for standard English. Misconception: mis-ordering the adverb 'just'.
- **(C)** 'he just eaten' drops the auxiliary 'has'. Misconception: leaving out the auxiliary of the present perfect.
- **(D)** 'is just eaten' uses the wrong auxiliary and makes a passive-looking form. Misconception: confusing the auxiliary 'has' with 'is'.

**Principle:** Present perfect with 'just' = a recently completed action with a present result; word order is has/have + just + past participle.

**Intuition hook:** 'He has just eaten' = it happened moments ago and still matters now.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Present Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect with 'just' and word order

questions.stem: I \_\_\_\_ TV peacefully when the lights suddenly \_\_\_\_ out.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The longer background action in progress uses the past continuous ('was watching'); the sudden, short interruption uses the simple past ('went out').

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'watched ... when' loses the 'in the middle of' meaning; it reads as a sequence, not an interruption. Misconception: using the simple past for a background action.
- **(C)** 'were going out' turns a sudden single event into an ongoing one. Misconception: continuous for a quick, completed interruption.
- **(D)** This reverses both forms. Misconception: swapping background and interruption.

**Principle:** Background action = past continuous; the event that interrupts it = simple past.

**Intuition hook:** The long thing was in progress (-ing) when the short thing struck (plain past).
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: When we finally reached the platform, the train \_\_\_\_ (already / leave).
questions.solution:
**Why:** The train leaving happened before we reached the platform, and 'already' confirms the earlier completion, so use the past perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'already left' drops the auxiliary 'had' that marks the earlier past event. Misconception: forgetting 'had' before an earlier action.
- 'has already left' is present perfect and cannot sit inside a past-time story. Misconception: mixing present perfect into a past narrative.

**Principle:** Of two past events, the earlier one takes the past perfect (had + past participle), especially with 'already'.

**Intuition hook:** The action that finished first wears the 'had' badge.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Past perfect for the earlier event

questions.stem: Which sentence is more natural?

options.label: A
options.text: 'First I brushed my teeth, and then I had gone to bed.'

options.label: B
options.text: 'First I brushed my teeth, and then I went to bed.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** When events are told in the order they happened and joined by 'then', the simple past is enough; the past perfect is unnecessary.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'had gone' wrongly marks the second, later action as the earlier one, which is backwards and needless. Misconception: over-using the past perfect for a plain sequence.

**Principle:** Use the past perfect only to signal that one past event came before another; a straightforward 'first... then' sequence needs only the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** Do not sprinkle 'had' everywhere; save it for the event that truly came first.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Correct the tense error: 'While she was reading, the lights suddenly went out and she was dropping her book.'
questions.answer: While she was reading, the lights suddenly went out and she dropped her book.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Dropping the book is a single, sudden, completed action, so it takes the simple past ('dropped'); only the ongoing background ('was reading') is continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'was dropping' turns an instant action into an ongoing one. Misconception: continuous for a sudden, one-moment action.

**Principle:** Sudden, completed actions use the simple past; only genuinely ongoing background actions use the past continuous.

**Intuition hook:** A book drops in an instant, so it cannot be 'in progress'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: I didn't recognise the town at all. It \_\_\_\_ a lot since my last visit.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The story is set in the past ('I didn't recognise'), and the changing happened before that past moment, so 'since' here requires the past perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'changed ... since' is incorrect; 'since' does not pair with the plain simple past. Misconception: simple past with 'since'.
- **(C)** 'was changing' describes an action in progress, not the completed change up to that past point. Misconception: continuous for a completed change.
- **(D)** 'has changed' is present perfect and clashes with the past setting 'I didn't recognise'. Misconception: present perfect inside a past narrative.

**Principle:** Inside a past-tense narrative, 'since' takes the past perfect, not the present perfect or simple past.

**Intuition hook:** Past story + 'since' = had + past participle.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Past perfect with 'since' in past narration

questions.stem: By the time the guests finally left, we \_\_\_\_ for six straight hours, and the kitchen was a total mess.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'By the time (past)' needs the past perfect, and 'for six straight hours' points to an ongoing activity, so the past perfect continuous fits both.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'cooked' has no auxiliary to mark 'before that past point', which 'by the time' demands. Misconception: simple past after 'by the time'.
- **(C)** 'were cooking' lacks the past perfect needed before the guests left. Misconception: past continuous with no 'had'.
- **(D)** 'have been cooking' is present perfect continuous and clashes with the past setting. Misconception: present perfect in a past story.

**Principle:** Past perfect continuous = an ongoing activity that continued up to a point in the past, often after 'by the time'.

**Intuition hook:** 'By the time' + how long + still going = had been -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Past perfect continuous for duration before a past point

questions.stem: By the time the ambulance arrived, the injured man \_\_\_\_ (already / lose) a great deal of blood.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The blood loss was complete before the ambulance arrived, and 'by the time' plus 'already' confirms the earlier completion, so use the past perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'already lost' omits 'had', the marker of the earlier past event. Misconception: dropping the auxiliary of the past perfect.
- 'has already lost' is present perfect and does not belong in a past-time story. Misconception: present perfect in past narration.

**Principle:** 'By the time (past), ... had already (done)' places the completed action before the later past point.

**Intuition hook:** Finished before the next past event? Use 'had'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: A student wants to say that he ate dinner AFTER getting home. He writes: 'When I reached home, I had eaten dinner.' Explain why this does not say what he means, and give the correct sentence.
questions.answer: 'Had eaten' means the dinner was already finished before he reached home. To mean he ate after arriving, use the simple past: 'When I reached home, I ate dinner.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The past perfect always signals the earlier of two past events, so 'had eaten' puts the dinner before the arrival, the opposite of his intended order.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping the past perfect reverses the true sequence of events. Misconception: thinking 'had' just makes a verb 'more past' rather than marking which event came first.

**Principle:** The past perfect marks the earlier of two past events; it changes the meaning, not just the 'feel'.

**Intuition hook:** 'Had done' = done before the other past thing, so check the order before you use it.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Meaning control with the past perfect

questions.stem: Based on this sentence, write the three events in the order they actually happened (earliest first): 'When the manager walked in, the team had submitted the report and were celebrating quietly.'
questions.answer: \1) The team submitted the report. 2) The manager walked in (while) 3) the team was celebrating.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Had submitted' (past perfect) is the earliest event; 'walked in' (simple past) is the reference point; 'were celebrating' (past continuous) was in progress at that reference point.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Reading the sentence in written order (walked in first) misses that 'had submitted' happened earliest. Misconception: assuming events are always narrated in time order.

**Principle:** Past perfect = earliest; simple past = the reference point; past continuous = in progress at that point.

**Intuition hook:** 'Had' comes first in time, even if it comes second in the sentence.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: When the teacher walked in, the students \_\_\_\_ (talk) so loudly that they did not even notice her.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The talking was already in progress when the teacher entered, which the past continuous captures; the added clause 'did not even notice her' confirms it was ongoing.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'talked' would read as if they started talking the moment she entered, contradicting 'did not even notice her'. Misconception: using the simple past for an action that was already in progress.

**Principle:** An action already in progress at a past moment uses the past continuous.

**Intuition hook:** They were mid-chatter when she walked in, so use '-ing'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Past continuous for an action in progress

questions.stem: One verb uses the past perfect where it is not needed. Find it and give the corrected verb: 'Yesterday morning I had finished my breakfast and rushed straight to school.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** This is a simple two-step sequence in the order it happened; the past perfect is unnecessary, so the simple past 'finished' is correct.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Leaving 'had finished' over-marks a plain sequence as if it needed to be set before another event. Misconception: using the past perfect whenever two past actions appear together.

**Principle:** The past perfect is only needed to show that one past event clearly preceded another; a plain 'and then' sequence does not require it.

**Intuition hook:** Two actions in a row are not automatically 'had'; keep it simple unless order needs marking.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: In which sentences is the past perfect used correctly and usefully? Choose ALL that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: 'By the time the firefighters arrived, the shed had burned down.'

options.label: B
options.text: 'I had eaten breakfast, and then I had brushed my teeth, and then I had left.'

options.label: C
options.text: 'She suddenly realised that she had forgotten her password.'

options.label: D
options.text: 'Yesterday I had gone to the market to buy vegetables.'

questions.solution:
**Why:** In A the burning finished before the firefighters arrived, and in C the forgetting happened before the realising; both correctly use the past perfect for the earlier event.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** This is a simple sequence, so every 'had' is over-used; it should be plain simple past. Misconception: past perfect for an ordinary chain of events.
- **(D)** A single past event with a time reference needs the simple past ('I went to the market yesterday'). Misconception: past perfect for a lone past action.

**Principle:** Use the past perfect only for an event that clearly happened before another past event or reference point.

**Intuition hook:** One earlier event behind a later one = 'had'; a plain list of steps = simple past.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Judging when the past perfect is justified

questions.stem: Describe the scene that was already happening as we set off. The sun \_\_\_\_ (shine) brightly and the birds \_\_\_\_ (sing) in the trees when we left the house.
questions.solution:
**Why:** These describe background conditions already in progress at the past moment we left, so both take the past continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'shone / sang' would suggest the shining and singing began the moment we left, rather than being already underway. Misconception: simple past for ongoing background scenery.

**Principle:** Ongoing background description at a past point uses the past continuous.

**Intuition hook:** Scene-setting that is already underway wants '-ing'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: The moment the final bell rang, the students \_\_\_\_ their books and \_\_\_\_ the classroom.
questions.solution:
**Why:** These are quick, completed actions that happened as a reaction to the bell, so the simple past is correct.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** The past continuous would mean they were only partway through when the bell rang, which is not the meaning. Misconception: continuous for finished reactions.
- **(C)** The past perfect wrongly places these actions before the bell rang. Misconception: past perfect for events that follow, not precede.
- **(D)** The simple present cannot narrate a past event. Misconception: present tense for a past action.

**Principle:** A quick, completed reaction to a past trigger uses the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** Bell rings, then they act and finish, so plain past for the actions.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Simple past for a completed reaction

questions.stem: 'When the coach entered, the players had hidden the birthday cake and were pretending to stretch.' Which event happened FIRST?

options.label: D
options.text: All three happened at the same time

questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Had hidden' (past perfect) is the earliest event; the coach entered afterwards, and the pretending was in progress at that moment.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** The coach entered after the cake was already hidden. Misconception: reading the first-mentioned clause as the first event.
- **(C)** The pretending was ongoing when the coach entered, so it did not start before the hiding. Misconception: treating the past continuous as the earliest event.
- **(D)** The past perfect specifically marks the hiding as earlier, so they were not simultaneous. Misconception: ignoring the ordering that tense provides.

**Principle:** The past perfect marks the earliest event, regardless of the order of mention.

**Intuition hook:** Find the 'had' and you have found what happened first.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Which sentence means the man was already gone before I got there? (1) 'When I arrived, he left.' (2) 'When I arrived, he had left.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Had left' places his leaving before my arrival; in sentence 1, 'left' suggests he left at or just after the moment I arrived.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** In sentence 1 the leaving lines up with or follows the arrival, not before it. Misconception: reading simple past as 'already earlier'.
- **(C)** The two sentences describe different orders of events. Misconception: assuming tense does not change the timeline.
- **(D)** Sentence 2 clearly gives the 'already gone' meaning. Misconception: overlooking the role of 'had'.

**Principle:** Past perfect vs. simple past after 'when' changes which event came first.

**Intuition hook:** 'He had left' = gone before you; 'he left' = went as/after you came.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Meaning contrast: past perfect vs. simple past

questions.stem: Correct this sentence: 'I was knowing the answer, so I raised my hand.'
questions.answer: I knew the answer, so I raised my hand.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Know' is a stative verb, so even in the past it uses the simple past ('knew'), not the past continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'was knowing' forces a state into the continuous. Misconception: stative verbs can take '-ing' in the past.

**Principle:** Stative verbs avoid the continuous in every tense, including the past.

**Intuition hook:** You cannot be 'in the middle of knowing', past or present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Before the internet \_\_\_\_ (become) common, people \_\_\_\_ (use) handwritten letters to keep in touch.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Both refer to a general past time; with 'before' the order is already clear, so the simple past is enough for both verbs.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'had become / had used' would over-mark a plain past-time description, since 'before' already shows the order. Misconception: adding the past perfect when a conjunction already orders events.

**Principle:** When 'before' or 'after' already shows the sequence, the simple past is usually sufficient.

**Intuition hook:** 'Before' does the ordering, so the verbs can stay simple.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Simple past with an ordering conjunction

questions.stem: When I was little, I \_\_\_\_ afraid of the dark, but I am not any more.
questions.solution:
**Why:** This is a past state that is no longer true, so the simple past 'was' is correct.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'am' contradicts 'when I was little' and 'not any more'. Misconception: present tense for a finished past state.
- **(C)** 'have been' suggests the fear continues to now, but it has ended. Misconception: present perfect for a state that has stopped.
- **(D)** 'was being' would imply deliberate temporary behaviour, not a genuine past state of fear. Misconception: continuous for a stative feeling.

**Principle:** A past state that no longer holds uses the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** Over and done with? Plain past.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Simple past for a former state

questions.stem: Explain the difference in meaning between these two sentences: (1) 'When the film started, we ate our popcorn.' (2) 'When the film started, we had eaten our popcorn.'
questions.answer: In (1) we ate the popcorn during or after the film started. In (2) 'had eaten' means the popcorn was already finished before the film started.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The past perfect in (2) places the eating before the film began; the simple past in (1) lines the eating up with or after the start.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Treating the two as identical ignores what 'had' does to the order. Misconception: assuming the past perfect is just a stylistic variant.

**Principle:** Past perfect vs. simple past controls whether an action finished before or happened during another past event.

**Intuition hook:** 'Had eaten' = popcorn gone before the film; 'ate' = popcorn during the film.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Combine into ONE sentence using the past perfect, keeping the meaning: 'The train left. Then we reached the platform.'
questions.answer: When we reached the platform, the train had already left.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The leaving happened first, so it takes the past perfect ('had left'); the later arrival takes the simple past.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'When we reached the platform, the train left' would wrongly suggest it left as we arrived. Misconception: using the simple past for the clearly earlier event.

**Principle:** The earlier of two combined past events takes the past perfect.

**Intuition hook:** Gone before you arrived = 'had left'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: The players were completely exhausted. They \_\_\_\_ (train — use the form that stresses the ongoing activity that caused it) hard for three hours before the coach let them rest.
questions.solution:
**Why:** An activity that continued for a stretch of time and led up to a past result (their exhaustion) uses the past perfect continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'trained' states a completed fact but does not stress the ongoing activity behind the exhaustion. Misconception: missing that the past perfect continuous best explains a past state.
- 'were training' lacks the 'had', so it does not sit clearly before the coach's decision. Misconception: past continuous with no earlier-time marking.

**Principle:** Past perfect continuous shows a continuous activity leading up to, and explaining, a later past situation.

**Intuition hook:** Tired then, because they had been -ing for hours.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Past perfect continuous for a past cause

questions.stem: Which option keeps the narrative consistent? 'Yesterday was strange. I woke up late, I \_\_\_\_ breakfast, and I \_\_\_\_ for the bus, but it never came.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The passage is a chain of completed past actions, so all verbs should stay in the simple past to match 'woke up' and 'came'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** The simple present breaks the past-tense narrative. Misconception: shifting into the present mid-story.
- **(C)** The past perfect wrongly signals these events came before the others, disrupting the sequence. Misconception: past perfect for a plain sequence.
- **(D)** The past continuous suggests these actions were merely in progress, not completed steps. Misconception: continuous for finished narrative actions.

**Principle:** A narrative of completed past events keeps a consistent simple past.

**Intuition hook:** Match the tense of the verbs around it; do not switch lanes mid-story.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Find the ONE verb that breaks the past-tense narrative and give the correction: 'The storm hit at midnight. Trees fell, the power went out, and everyone rushes to shut the windows.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The whole passage is in the simple past ('hit', 'fell', 'went'), so 'rushes' is an inconsistent shift into the present and must become 'rushed'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Leaving 'rushes' mixes present and past in one narrative. Misconception: losing tense control across a passage.

**Principle:** Keep one consistent tense throughout a narrative unless the meaning requires a shift.

**Intuition hook:** One present-tense verb in a past story sticks out; make it match.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Past Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Spotting a tense shift in a passage

questions.stem: 'The phone is ringing.' 'Oh, I \_\_\_\_ answer it.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The speaker decides to answer at the moment of speaking, and a spontaneous decision uses 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'am going to' signals a decision made earlier, but this choice is made right now. Misconception: confusing a plan with a spur-of-the-moment decision.
- **(C)** 'am answering' suggests a fixed prior arrangement, which a ringing phone is not. Misconception: present continuous for an instant decision.
- **(D)** 'answer' is the simple present and cannot express this future action. Misconception: present tense for a future decision.

**Principle:** A decision made at the moment of speaking uses 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** Decide on the spot? Say 'I will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: You can see it in the sky right now — those heavy dark clouds mean it \_\_\_\_ rain very soon.
questions.solution:
**Why:** When a prediction is based on present evidence you can see now, 'going to' is the natural choice.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will' makes a prediction too, but 'going to' is preferred when there is visible present evidence for it. Misconception: ignoring that visible evidence points to 'going to'.
- **(C)** 'rains' is the simple present for habits or schedules, not a prediction. Misconception: present simple for a forecast.
- **(D)** 'is raining' means it is raining now, but it has not started yet. Misconception: present continuous for something not yet happening.

**Principle:** A prediction based on present evidence uses 'be going to'.

**Intuition hook:** If you can see it coming, it is 'going to' happen.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Hurry up! According to the timetable, the train \_\_\_\_ (leave) at exactly 7:15.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Fixed timetables and schedules use the simple present, even for future events.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'is leaving' suits a personal arrangement, but a public timetable uses the simple present. Misconception: continuous for a scheduled service.
- 'will leave' is a general prediction, not the fixed schedule the timetable states. Misconception: 'will' for a timetabled event.

**Principle:** Timetables and schedules use the simple present for future events.

**Intuition hook:** If a timetable prints it, use the plain present: 'the train leaves at...'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: I can't meet you on Friday afternoon. I \_\_\_\_ my dentist at 4 p.m. — the appointment is already booked.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A fixed personal arrangement with a set time and place uses the present continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will see' suggests a decision made now, not an appointment already booked. Misconception: 'will' for a pre-arranged plan.
- **(C)** 'see' is the simple present for habits, not this single future appointment. Misconception: present simple for a one-time arrangement.
- **(D)** 'will be seeing' (future continuous) over-complicates a simple booked appointment. Misconception: future continuous for a plain arrangement.

**Principle:** Fixed future arrangements (with a time/place agreed) use the present continuous.

**Intuition hook:** Already booked with a time? Use 'I am -ing'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: By this time next year, I \_\_\_\_ from secondary school.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'By (a future time)' with an action completed before that point uses the future perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will graduate' states a future action but does not stress that it is finished by that point. Misconception: simple future where completion-by-a-deadline is meant.
- **(C)** 'am graduating' is a present arrangement, not a completion by a future deadline. Misconception: present continuous for a future-perfect idea.
- **(D)** 'graduate' is the simple present and cannot express this. Misconception: present tense for a future completion.

**Principle:** Future perfect (will have + past participle) = an action completed before a future point.

**Intuition hook:** 'By \[future time\]' + already done = will have done.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Future perfect for completion by a deadline

questions.stem: Don't worry about the money. I \_\_\_\_ (pay) you back next week, I promise.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A promise uses 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'am going to pay' states an intention, but 'I promise' calls for the promise form 'will'. Misconception: 'going to' for a solemn promise.
- 'pay' is the simple present and cannot carry this future promise. Misconception: present tense for a promise.

**Principle:** Promises use 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** 'I promise' pairs naturally with 'I will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Please don't call me at 8 tonight — I'll be right in the middle of it. I \_\_\_\_ dinner then.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a specific future time.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will have' (future perfect/possession) does not express an action in progress. Misconception: mixing up future perfect and future continuous.
- **(C)** 'have' is the simple present, wrong for a future moment in progress. Misconception: present tense for a future ongoing action.
- **(D)** 'had' is the simple past, the wrong direction in time. Misconception: past for a future action.

**Principle:** Future continuous (will be + -ing) = an action in progress at a point in the future.

**Intuition hook:** 'At 8 I'll be mid-action' = will be -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Future continuous for an in-progress future action

questions.stem: I've finally made up my mind. I \_\_\_\_ learn to play the guitar this year.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A decision already made (an intention) uses 'be going to', which 'I've finally made up my mind' signals.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will' fits a decision made at the moment of speaking, but this decision is already made. Misconception: 'will' for a pre-formed intention.
- **(C)** 'learn' is the simple present and cannot express this plan. Misconception: present tense for an intention.
- **(D)** 'am learning' suggests a fixed arrangement already in progress, not a fresh intention. Misconception: present continuous for a plan with no fixed details.

**Principle:** 'Be going to' expresses an intention or a decision already made before speaking.

**Intuition hook:** Already decided in your head? 'I'm going to'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: The city museum \_\_\_\_ (open) at 9 a.m. and \_\_\_\_ (close) at 6 p.m. every day of the week.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Regular opening hours are a fixed schedule, so both verbs use the simple present.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'is opening / is closing' would wrongly make a permanent schedule sound temporary. Misconception: continuous for regular hours.
- 'will open / will close' treats a fixed timetable as a one-off prediction. Misconception: 'will' for scheduled hours.

**Principle:** Regular schedules and opening hours use the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** Opening hours are routine, so keep them in the plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Simple present for a fixed schedule

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a plan that is already arranged for a definite time? (1) 'I am visiting my grandmother this weekend.' (2) 'I will visit my grandmother someday.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present continuous ('am visiting') with 'this weekend' marks a definite, arranged plan; 'will ... someday' is a vague, unarranged intention.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'will ... someday' has no fixed time and no arrangement. Misconception: reading 'will' as a firm plan.
- **(C)** The two express different degrees of certainty and arrangement. Misconception: treating the futures as equal.
- **(D)** Sentence 1 clearly describes an arranged plan. Misconception: missing the arrangement in the present continuous.

**Principle:** Present continuous = arranged, definite future plan; 'will' can be a vague or spontaneous future.

**Intuition hook:** A plan on the calendar is 'I am -ing'; a maybe-one-day is 'I will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: The film starts at 8 p.m. and runs for two hours, so by 10:30 it \_\_\_\_.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'By 10:30' with an action finished before that point uses the future perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will end' does not stress that it is already over by 10:30. Misconception: simple future for a by-then completion.
- **(C)** 'ends' is the simple present, wrong for this completion. Misconception: present tense for a future-perfect meaning.
- **(D)** 'is ending' means ending right now, not finished by a future time. Misconception: present continuous for a future completion.

**Principle:** Future perfect = completed before a stated future time.

**Intuition hook:** 'By \[future time\], it will already be done' = will have + participle.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Correct the future form: 'Look out! You will drop the vase!' (You can see it is about to slip from his hands.)
questions.answer: Look out! You are going to drop the vase!
questions.solution:
**Why:** When something is clearly about to happen, judged from what you can see right now, use 'be going to', not 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'will drop' sounds like a general prediction rather than an imminent event based on present evidence. Misconception: 'will' for something visibly about to occur.

**Principle:** An imminent event, judged from present evidence, uses 'be going to'.

**Intuition hook:** About to happen before your eyes = 'going to'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: According to the official timetable, our final exam \_\_\_\_ next Monday at 10 a.m.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A fixed, scheduled event can be stated with the simple present of 'to be'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'is being' is not used for a scheduled event like this. Misconception: continuous of 'be' for a timetabled event.
- **(C)** 'will be being' is not a natural English form here. Misconception: over-building the verb phrase.
- **(D)** 'was' is past, but the exam is in the future. Misconception: past tense for a future schedule.

**Principle:** Scheduled events can be expressed with the simple present ('The exam is on Monday').

**Intuition hook:** Fixed on the schedule? 'The exam is on Monday' works fine.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Simple present for a scheduled event

questions.stem: Many scientists believe that robots \_\_\_\_ (do) most dangerous jobs in the future.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A general prediction about the future uses 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'are doing' is present continuous and cannot express a future prediction. Misconception: present continuous for a general forecast.
- 'do' is the simple present for habits, not a prediction. Misconception: present tense for the future.

**Principle:** General predictions about the future use 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** A forecast with no present evidence leans on 'will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: A: 'We've run out of milk.' B: 'Oh, \_\_\_\_ some on my way home.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** Speaker B reacts to information just heard and decides on the spot, so 'will' is correct.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'I'm going to buy' suggests a plan made earlier, but this is a fresh reaction to new information. Misconception: 'going to' for a spur-of-the-moment reaction.
- **(C)** 'I buy' is the simple present for habits, not this decision. Misconception: present tense for an instant decision.
- **(D)** 'I'm buying' implies an existing arrangement, which there is none. Misconception: present continuous for an on-the-spot choice.

**Principle:** A decision made in reaction to what you just heard uses 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** Just found out and decided right then? 'I'll'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: We \_\_\_\_ our new neighbours to dinner on Saturday; the table is booked and everything is arranged.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A fully arranged future plan with a set day uses the present continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will invite' suggests a decision made now, not a settled arrangement. Misconception: 'will' for an arranged plan.
- **(C)** 'invite' is the simple present for habits. Misconception: present simple for a single arranged event.
- **(D)** 'will be inviting' (future continuous) is heavier than this simple arrangement needs. Misconception: future continuous for a plain plan.

**Principle:** Present continuous marks a fixed, arranged future plan.

**Intuition hook:** 'Everything is arranged' calls for 'we are -ing'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Present continuous for an arranged plan

questions.stem: For a plan already arranged with friends, which is more natural, and why? 'I will meet my friends at the mall tomorrow; we arranged it last week.'
questions.answer: The present continuous is more natural for a plan arranged in advance: 'I am meeting my friends at the mall tomorrow.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** Because the plan was arranged last week, the present continuous fits better than 'will', which usually signals a decision made at the moment of speaking.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'will meet' is not wrong grammar, but it hides the fact that the plan was already arranged. Misconception: using 'will' for pre-arranged plans and losing the 'already arranged' meaning.

**Principle:** For arrangements made in advance, the present continuous is more natural than 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** Arranged with people, in advance? Prefer 'I am meeting'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: I will call you as soon as I \_\_\_\_ home.
questions.solution:
**Why:** After time words like 'as soon as', 'when', and 'after', the future is expressed with the simple present, not 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will reach' puts 'will' inside the time clause, which English avoids. Misconception: doubling 'will' in a time clause.
- **(C)** 'am reaching' is a present arrangement, not the time-clause form. Misconception: continuous inside a time clause.
- **(D)** 'will have reached' over-builds a simple time clause. Misconception: future perfect where the simple present is needed.

**Principle:** In future time clauses (after when, as soon as, before, after), use the simple present, not 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** Never use two 'wills': keep the time clause in the plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: If it \_\_\_\_ (rain) tomorrow, we will move the picnic indoors.
questions.solution:
**Why:** In a first-conditional 'if' clause about the future, the verb is in the simple present, not 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'will rain' wrongly puts 'will' inside the if-clause; only the main clause takes 'will'. Misconception: 'will' after 'if'.

**Principle:** In a future 'if' clause, use the simple present; put 'will' only in the result clause.

**Intuition hook:** 'If it rains, we will...' – the 'if' half stays plain present.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: This time tomorrow, we \_\_\_\_ high above the Atlantic Ocean on our flight to New York.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'This time tomorrow' points to a moment when the action will already be in progress, which is the future continuous.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'will fly' presents the flight as a whole event, not as in progress at that exact moment. Misconception: simple future where an in-progress future is meant.
- **(C)** 'fly' is the simple present for habits or schedules. Misconception: present tense for a future ongoing action.
- **(D)** 'are flying' suggests an arrangement, but 'this time tomorrow' calls for the in-progress future. Misconception: present continuous instead of future continuous.

**Principle:** 'This time tomorrow / at 9 tomorrow' with an action in progress uses the future continuous.

**Intuition hook:** Mid-action at a future moment = will be -ing.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

fields.Cognitive skill: Future continuous with a future time point

questions.stem: Are both acceptable ways to predict the weather? (1) 'I think it will snow tonight.' (2) 'I think it is going to snow tonight.'
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Will' and 'be going to' can both express predictions; with a general opinion like 'I think', either is fine.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'going to' is also a valid prediction form, so (2) is fine. Misconception: thinking only 'will' can predict.
- **(B)** 'will' is a valid prediction form, so (1) is fine. Misconception: thinking only 'going to' can predict.
- **(D)** Both are grammatical predictions. Misconception: rejecting two correct forms.

**Principle:** For predictions, 'will' and 'be going to' often overlap and are both acceptable.

**Intuition hook:** To predict, either 'will' or 'going to' usually works; evidence just tips it toward 'going to'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: I \_\_\_\_ always be there for you, no matter what happens.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A heartfelt promise about the future uses 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** 'am going to' states an intention but sounds flatter than a promise. Misconception: 'going to' for a solemn promise.
- **(C)** 'am' is the simple present and cannot carry this future promise. Misconception: present tense for a future promise.
- **(D)** 'am being' wrongly turns a permanent commitment into temporary behaviour. Misconception: continuous of 'be' for a lasting promise.

**Principle:** Promises and commitments about the future use 'will'.

**Intuition hook:** A vow reaches for 'I will'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: Correct this sentence: 'When I will grow up, I will become a pilot.'
questions.answer: When I grow up, I will become a pilot.
questions.solution:
**Why:** The time clause after 'when' takes the simple present; only the main clause keeps 'will'.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'when I will grow up' puts 'will' inside a time clause, which English does not allow. Misconception: 'will' after 'when'.

**Principle:** Do not use 'will' in a future time clause; use the simple present.

**Intuition hook:** 'When I grow up' (plain present), then 'I will become' (will).
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: A: 'What are your plans for the summer?' B: 'Well, I \_\_\_\_ a coding course in June — I've already enrolled — and after that I \_\_\_\_ visit my cousins, though I haven't fixed any dates.'

options.label: D
options.text: am going to take / am visiting

questions.solution:
**Why:** The enrolled course is a fixed arrangement (present continuous, 'am taking'); the unfixed cousin visit is an intention (be going to, 'am going to visit').

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(B)** Both 'will' forms miss the difference between a booked arrangement and a loose intention. Misconception: treating all futures as one.
- **(C)** The simple present cannot express these future plans. Misconception: present tense for future plans.
- **(D)** This swaps the forms: the fixed, enrolled course should be the present continuous, not the visit. Misconception: matching the arrangement form to the wrong plan.

**Principle:** Fixed arrangement = present continuous; intention with no fixed details = be going to.

**Intuition hook:** Booked = 'I am -ing'; just intending = 'I'm going to'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Future Tense Nuance

questions.stem: She \_\_\_\_ three cups of coffee so far today, and it is only 10 a.m.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'So far today' names a period that is not yet finished, so the present perfect is required.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'drank ... so far today' is wrong; an unfinished period cannot take the plain simple past. Misconception: simple past inside an ongoing time period.
- **(C)** 'drinks' is the simple present for habits, not this running total. Misconception: present simple for an up-to-now count.
- **(D)** 'is drinking' means right at this second, not across the morning. Misconception: present continuous for a period up to now.

**Principle:** An unfinished time period (today, this week, so far) takes the present perfect.

**Intuition hook:** If the day is not over, the count lives in 'has done'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect for an unfinished period

questions.stem: They \_\_\_\_ (know) each other for more than twenty years.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'For more than twenty years' up to now, with the stative verb 'know', uses the present perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'know ... for twenty years' wrongly uses the simple present for a stretch up to now. Misconception: present simple with a 'for'-duration.
- 'knew' would suggest they no longer know each other. Misconception: simple past for a friendship that continues.

**Principle:** 'For + duration up to now' uses the present perfect, even with stative verbs.

**Intuition hook:** 'For twenty years and still counting' = have known.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: Shakespeare \_\_\_\_ many of the most famous plays in the English language.
questions.solution:
**Why:** Shakespeare's life and writing are completely finished, so his work is described with the simple past.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'has written' wrongly implies the writing is still connected to now or could continue, but he can write no more. Misconception: present perfect for a person whose life is over.
- **(C)** 'had written' needs a second, later past event to sit before. Misconception: past perfect with no second past reference.
- **(D)** 'writes' is the simple present, but he does not write now. Misconception: present tense for a finished body of work.

**Principle:** The present perfect implies a link to the present; a finished life or period uses the simple past.

**Intuition hook:** A living artist 'has painted'; a departed one 'painted'.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: Correct this sentence: 'I have seen that film last night.'
questions.answer: I saw that film last night.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'Last night' is a definite finished time, which cannot combine with the present perfect, so use the simple past.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Keeping 'have seen ... last night' pairs the present perfect with a finished time word. Misconception: present perfect with a specific past time.

**Principle:** The present perfect never takes a definite past-time expression (yesterday, last night, in 2019).

**Intuition hook:** Name the exact time and you must switch to the simple past.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

fields.Cognitive skill: Present perfect vs. simple past with a time word

questions.stem: \_\_\_\_ you ever \_\_\_\_ to Japan? I mean at any point in your life.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A question about life experience up to now uses the present perfect, and 'been' means went and came back.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** The simple past asks about a specific past occasion, not lifelong experience. Misconception: simple past for an 'ever in your life' question.
- **(C)** 'gone' would mean the person is still in Japan now, which does not fit. Misconception: confusing 'been' (returned) with 'gone' (still away).
- **(D)** 'Do you go' asks about a habit, not experience. Misconception: present simple for a life experience.

**Principle:** Present perfect + 'ever' asks about experience at any time up to now; 'been' = went and returned.

**Intuition hook:** 'Have you ever been...?' asks about your whole life so far.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: This is the best pizza I \_\_\_\_ (ever / eat)!
questions.solution:
**Why:** A superlative ('the best ... ever') looks back over all experience up to now, which is the present perfect.

**Distractor analysis:**

- 'ever ate' uses the simple past where the 'up to now' experience pattern needs the present perfect. Misconception: simple past in a 'best ... ever' structure.

**Principle:** Superlative + 'ever' (the best I have ever...) uses the present perfect.

**Intuition hook:** 'Best ... I've ever had' is a fixed present-perfect pattern.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: You've missed her by a minute. She \_\_\_\_ left the building.
questions.solution:
**Why:** A very recent action with a present result uses the present perfect with 'just': has + just + past participle.

**Distractor analysis:**

- **(A)** 'she just left' drops the auxiliary needed here for the present-result meaning. Misconception: leaving out 'has'.
- **(C)** 'just has left' mis-orders the adverb. Misconception: wrong placement of 'just'.
- **(D)** 'had just left' is past perfect and needs a second past event. Misconception: past perfect with no second past point.

**Principle:** Present perfect with 'just' = a moment-ago action that still matters now.

**Intuition hook:** 'She has just left' = gone seconds ago, so you missed her.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: Explain when you would use each sentence: (1) 'I have lost my umbrella.' (2) 'I lost my umbrella.'
questions.answer: (1) The present perfect stresses the present result: it is still lost, I do not have it now. (2) The simple past just reports a past event, perhaps one that is now over (I may have found it since).
questions.solution:
**Why:** The present perfect connects the past action to the present situation; the simple past simply places the event in the past with no stated link to now.

**Distractor analysis:**

- Treating the two as identical misses that the present perfect signals a result that still holds. Misconception: assuming 'have lost' and 'lost' always mean the same.

**Principle:** Present perfect = past action with present relevance; simple past = past event, no stated present link.

**Intuition hook:** 'I have lost it' = still gone now; 'I lost it' = just a past fact.
topics: Grammar > Verb Tenses > Perfect Tense Reasoning

questions.stem: By the time the teacher collected the answer sheets, most students \_\_\_\_ only half of the questions.
questions.solution:
**Why:** 'By the time (past)' with an action completed before that past point uses the past perfect.
